description: Test your knowledge of Thoracic cage anatomy, including the sternum, ribs, and thoracic vertebrae with clinical correlations.

cards.text: What is the sternal angle (Angle of Louis) and why is it clinically important?
cards.answer: The sternal angle is the palpable ridge where the manubrium meets the body of the sternum (~5 cm below the jugular notch). It marks the level of the 2nd costal cartilage, tracheal bifurcation, aortic arch, T4/T5 intervertebral disc, and the boundary between superior and inferior mediastinum.

tip.tip: Remember: Sternal angle = your anatomical GPS for multiple vital structures

cards.text: Name the three parts of the sternum from top to bottom.
cards.answer: Manubrium (upper broad part with jugular notch), Body (longest part with transverse ridges), Xiphoid process (small pointed projection, ossifies by age 40).

cards.text: How are ribs classified based on their anterior attachment?
cards.answer: True ribs (1–7) attach directly to sternum; False ribs (8–10) attach indirectly via the rib above; Floating ribs (11–12) have no anterior attachment—free anterior ends.

tip.tip: TFF rule: True (1-7) direct, False (8-10) indirect, Floating (11-12) free

cards.text: What are the five key features of a typical rib (ribs 3–9)?
cards.answer: Head (with two articular facets separated by a crest), Neck, Tubercle, Shaft/body (with a sharp angle), and Costal groove on the inferior inner surface (shelters intercostal vessels and nerve).

tip.tip: Head-Neck-Tubercle-Angle-Shaft = HNTAS (and remember the costal groove)

cards.text: What makes the 1st rib unique, and what is its clinical significance?
cards.answer: The 1st rib is short, flat, horizontally oriented with a single head facet. Its upper surface has grooves for the subclavian artery and vein separated by the scalene tubercle. A fractured 1st rib suggests severe trauma and raises concern for vascular injury.

tip.tip: 1st rib = the strongest and best-protected; if broken, always suspect major trauma and vascular damage

cards.text: Why is the xiphoid process dangerous during CPR?
cards.answer: Direct pressure on the xiphoid process during CPR can fracture it and lacerate the underlying liver, causing severe hemorrhage. Proper hand placement is at the junction of the xiphoid with the body of the sternum.

tip.tip: Xiphoid = danger zone; aim for safe sternal placement above it

cards.text: How do thoracic vertebrae articulate with ribs?
cards.answer: A typical thoracic vertebra (T2–T8) has superior and inferior demifacets (half-facets) on each side of the body. A typical rib head spans two vertebral bodies, articulating with the inferior demifacet of the vertebra above and the superior demifacet of the corresponding vertebra.

tip.tip: One rib = two vertebrae; demifacets = each vertebra gets half a rib's attachment

cards.text: What are the features of the 11th and 12th ribs (floating ribs)?
cards.answer: They are short, have single facets on their heads (articulate with only one vertebra), lack a neck, tubercle, and angle, and have free anterior ends with no sternal attachment.

tip.tip: Floating ribs = the minimalists; only head + shaft, nothing else
